title: How to Soundproof an Apartment Without Losing Your Deposit
meta_description: How to soundproof an apartment without damage: seal gaps, add soft surfaces, quiet shared walls and talk to neighbors. Renter-friendly fixes.
body_html:
You cannot rebuild the walls of a rental, but you can make a noisy apartment noticeably quieter without drills, glue, or deposit deductions. The key is understanding where sound gets in and choosing fixes that match the problem. Here is how to soundproof an apartment the renter-friendly way.

First, figure out what kind of noise you have

Different noise needs different fixes, so spend a day paying attention to it.

  • Airborne noise travels through the air: voices, TVs, music, traffic, barking. It sneaks through gaps and thin surfaces.
  • Impact noise comes from something hitting the structure: footsteps above you, doors slamming, furniture dragging. It travels through floors and walls.
  • Echo inside your unit makes everything sound louder, especially in rooms with hard floors and bare walls.

A useful rule of thumb: sealing gaps and adding mass helps block sound, while soft materials mostly absorb echo. Thin acoustic foam panels can make a room sound less echoey, but on their own they do little to stop a neighbor's TV.

Seal the gaps around your front door

Sound leaks through any opening air can pass through, and the front door is often the biggest offender, especially the gap at the bottom.

  • Add a door sweep or draft stopper to the bottom of the door. Slide-on or adhesive styles avoid screws. Check that the door still closes and latches easily.
  • Apply adhesive weatherstripping around the door frame where the door meets the jamb. Foam or rubber strips usually peel off cleanly when you move, but test a small piece first.
  • Do the same for interior doors, like a bedroom that faces a noisy hallway or living room.

Weatherstripping also cuts drafts, which can help with heating and cooling. Ask your landlord before modifying an exterior door, and never block or impede a door you may need to exit in an emergency.

Quiet your windows

If traffic or street noise is the problem, focus on windows.

  • Hang heavy, lined curtains that cover the whole window frame and extend past the edges. Thick, dense fabrics work better than light ones. Tension rods or adhesive hooks can work if you cannot drill.
  • Seal drafty gaps with removable weatherstripping or rope caulk, which presses into gaps and pulls out later.
  • Consider window inserts for serious street noise. These sit inside the frame and add a second layer of glazing. They cost more, but many are designed to be removable.
  • Close windows and use a fan or AC for airflow during noisy hours.

Keep at least one window in each bedroom able to open, since windows can be an emergency exit.

Make shared walls less noisy

For a neighbor's TV or conversations coming through a wall, add mass and distance.

  • Put a full bookcase against the shared wall. Books are dense and the air gap behind the shelf helps. Anchor tall furniture according to your lease rules.
  • Move your bed or desk away from the shared wall if the room allows.
  • Hang a thick tapestry, quilt, or sound-absorbing blanket on the wall using damage-free hooks. This mostly reduces echo but helps a bit with mid-range sounds.
  • Use freestanding acoustic panels on stands or leaned against the wall instead of gluing them up.

Short on space? Our small apartment design ideas show how to place furniture so it works harder.

Soften the floors

If you have hard floors, adding soft layers reduces echo in your unit and can cut the impact noise you send downstairs.

  • Use large area rugs with a thick rug pad. The pad does a lot of the work. Dense felt or rubber-and-felt pads are better than thin grip mats.
  • Put felt pads under chairs and furniture so dragging does not scrape and thump.
  • Use rubber or anti-vibration pads under washing machines, speakers, and subwoofers.

Unfortunately, you cannot do much about the neighbor upstairs from your side, except talk to them (see below). Rugs, along with reasonable quiet hours, are a fair thing to ask about.

Mask what you cannot block

When the noise is unavoidable, covering it with a steadier sound can make it far less disruptive, especially for sleep.

  • A white noise machine or fan produces a consistent sound that makes sudden noises less jarring.
  • Foam earplugs or sleep earbuds are cheap and effective for nights.
  • Noise-canceling headphones help most with steady, low sounds like traffic hum or HVAC.

Place a white noise machine between you and the source of the noise, such as near the bedroom door or the shared wall, and keep the volume at a comfortable level. Experiment for a few nights; some people prefer fan-like sounds over pure static.

Which fix for which noise

Noise problemBest first fixes
Hallway voices and footstepsDoor sweep, weatherstripping around the door frame
Traffic and street noiseHeavy curtains, window gaps sealed, window inserts
Neighbor's TV through the wallBookcase on shared wall, move the bed, white noise
Echo in your own unitRugs with thick pads, curtains, soft furniture, wall hangings
Footsteps from upstairsTalk to the neighbor, white noise, earplugs at night

Talk to your neighbors and landlord

Many noise problems are easier to solve with a conversation than with gear. Most people do not realize how much they can be heard.

Try something like: "Hi, I'm in [unit]. I don't think you realize it, but sound carries a lot between our places, especially after [time]. Would you mind keeping it down after then? Let me know if I'm ever too loud too."

If that does not work, check your lease for quiet hours or noise rules and report ongoing problems to your landlord in writing. Keep a simple log of dates and times. Rules vary by building and city, so check your lease and local ordinances. For more on getting along in shared buildings, see our apartment living tips, and if you are still apartment hunting, add noise to your list of questions to ask before signing a lease.

Frequently asked questions

Do acoustic foam panels soundproof a room?

Not really. Foam panels absorb echo inside a room, which can make it sound quieter, but they do little to block sound coming through walls. Sealing gaps and adding mass work better for blocking.

Can I soundproof without damaging the walls?

Yes. Door sweeps, removable weatherstripping, heavy curtains on tension rods, rugs, bookcases, and white noise all work without holes or glue. Test adhesives on a small spot first.

What is the cheapest way to reduce apartment noise?

A door sweep, weatherstripping, earplugs, and a fan for white noise are inexpensive and often make a noticeable difference.

Will my landlord let me install soundproofing?

Ask before doing anything permanent. Most landlords will not mind removable fixes, but get approval in writing for anything that alters the unit.
